html:
The new capital that Emperor Wen of the Sui began in 582, just southeast of the old Han city of Chang'an, in the Wei River valley of northwest China. The Sui called it Daxing; the Tang renamed it Chang'an and made it the greatest city of its age, with perhaps a million people.

It was laid out as a huge walled grid. A broad avenue ran from the palace in the north to the south gate, and the streets cut the city into a hundred or so walled wards, closed at night. Two great markets, East and West, drew merchants from along the Silk Road, including Sogdians, Persians and Turks. Buddhist monks like Xuanzang translated scripture here.

Its plan was copied abroad. Japan built Nara and then Heian-kyō (Kyoto) as smaller versions of it. The city was sacked during the An Lushan Rebellion and wrecked when the Tang fell in the early 900s. The modern city of Xi'an stands on part of the site.
